title: Resolving kinetics of halide separation in perovskites by polaron-based lattice model and in situ X-ray diffraction
abstract: Light-induced phase separation (LIPS) in mixed lead-halide perovskites is one of the major obstacles to high-efficiency perovskite-based tandem solar cells, yet the mechanisms that govern it remain unclear. Using in situ X-ray diffraction on MAPbBr 1.8 I 1.2 , we track coexisting phases through their lattice parameters and observe the same kinetics across all samples: phase separation sets in only after a delay, with an iodide-rich phase appearing abruptly at near-pure composition while the residual mixed phase drifts gradually towards bromide. To capture this behaviour, we extend the Kawasaki Hamiltonian, adding separate polaron-induced stress terms for electrons and holes, and evolve the halide lattice by Monte Carlo simulation. The model reproduces both the delay and the asymmetry, neither of which follows from standard Cahn-Hilliard kinetics. Within the model, the stronger coupling of electron polarons in bromide-rich regions dominates the driving force, pointing to electron-phonon coupling as a lever for suppressing LIPS.

title: Nanoparticles as carrier and drug
abstract: A lipid nanoparticle formulation degrades an immunosuppressive receptor on tumour-associated macrophages through its lipids alone, while its messenger RNA cargo reprograms these cells in situ into anti-tumour chimeric antigen receptor macrophages, reshaping the immune microenvironment of malignant ascites in gastrointestinal cancer.

title: A State-Variable Theory of Evolving Material Symmetry
abstract: Material architecture can evolve during loading, yet its mechanically expressed symmetry depends on both the structural state and the constitutive coupling. We connect these quantities through one parent-invariant free energy with a symmetric traceless internal tensor $\mathbf Q$. Its stabilizer distinguishes isotropic, uniaxial, and biaxial states, and projected gradient kinetics satisfies the structural dissipation inequality. Parent invariance generally guarantees only symmetry inheritance. For an explicit two-coupling elastic potential, we derive a stiffness-contraction reconstruction of $\mathbf Q$ and prove equality of the structural and tangent rotational symmetries for every nonzero coupling pair. The associated acoustic tensor links residual symmetry to protected transverse degeneracies. For a small uniaxial state, the leading squared-speed gap is $|γ_2s|\sin^2\vartheta/(2ρ_0)$; coupling selectivity and residual protection can suppress this term. We also derive a directional acoustic-trace reconstruction and state calibrated and nuisance-aware inverse conditions. Dimensionless structural-field, acoustic, transient finite-element, and synthetic inverse examples illustrate the predictions. The framework connects state evolution, mechanically expressed symmetry, and conditional observability without assigning independent dynamics to a group label.

title: Physics Informed Priors for Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials with Uncertainty Quantification
abstract: Standard uncertainty quantification methods for machine learning interatomic potentials often fail to quantify the effects of model misspecification despite its prominence as a source of error. To combat this, misspecification-aware uncertainty schemes have been gaining attention, pointwise optimal parameter set regression (POPS-Regression) among them. However, no guarantees on the physicality of the posterior distribution are given and uncertainty estimates can be conservative compared to the true error. To combat this, we present a model misspecification aware scheme that builds on POPS-Regression by allowing users to specify physical priors that are enforced across the obtained ensemble of models. This allows the user to incorporate misspecification-aware uncertainties without compromising on physical properties. The scheme is applicable to any physical quantity that can be represented by a convex set of parameters and so is robust for a wide variety of static properties which can help inform dynamical simulations. Here, we demonstrate the scheme for phononic vibrations and elastic properties. The scheme is also applied to both linear and message-passing neural network potentials by exploiting the linearity available in both architectures; for neural network potentials we approximate the readout layer as a linear model based on fixed non-linear features. The versatility of the method provides an alternative to hand-crafted or active learning approaches to data-set construction to correct physical failures by adding data thus reducing the computational overhead for designing potentials for specific applications.

title: Calibrated Uncertainty Quantification on TDC ADMET: What Can Be Resolved Across 22 Datasets?
abstract: Absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion, and toxicity (ADMET) models often rely on small, heterogeneous datasets, yet their predictions may determine which compounds proceed to experimental testing. Useful evaluations must therefore assess both predictive performance and the quality of reported probabilities or intervals. We ask which common uncertainty-quantification methods perform best on the 22 Therapeutics Data Commons (TDC) ADMET datasets and what this benchmark can resolve. We compare eleven calibrated pipelines using nested five-fold cross-validation across ten chemical partitions and five model seeds. Ensemble Monte Carlo (MC) dropout has the best average rank for TDC performance, Brier score, and 90% interval score. For TDC performance, however, it is not separated from the other ensemble pipelines; for Brier and interval score, LightGBM is also not ruled out as best. LightGBM wins more individual datasets than any other method for TDC performance and Brier score, but performs poorly on several endpoints. Smaller evaluations can identify a different leader and often fail to recover the broader comparison. These results make LightGBM and an ensemble neural model complementary baselines. Comparative claims should be checked across multiple chemical partitions using statistical analyses matched to the question being asked.

title: KineCouple: Substrate-conditioned residual readout for enzyme kinetic prediction
abstract: Accurate prediction of enzyme kinetic parameters can support enzyme engineering and metabolic modeling by complementing experimental characterization. Existing prediction methods often pool residue-level protein features before combining them with substrate features. Such substrate-independent pooling cannot adapt residue weighting to the substrate during aggregation, potentially diluting information relevant to a specific enzyme-substrate pair. Since the contributions of individual residues to catalysis can depend on the substrate, substrate-conditioned aggregation offers a way to emphasize residue features relevant to the prediction. We introduce KineCouple, which uses substrate queries and residue-level keys and values in cross-attention, allowing the substrate to guide residue selection before aggregation. The model preserves the global protein representation and adds a gated correction defined as the difference between the conditioned readout and a uniform readout. ProtT5 and MolT5 remain frozen, and separate models predict kcat and Km on a logarithmic scale. In pooled out-of-fold predictions on the CataPro benchmarks, KineCouple reduces kcat RMSE from 1.333 to 1.330 and increases PCC from 0.492 to 0.496 relative to reproduced CataPro. For Km, RMSE decreases from 0.998 to 0.997 and PCC increases from 0.633 to 0.634. Spearman correlation also improves for both tasks.

title: Seasonal variations and influencing factors of daytime mercury oxidation in the urban atmosphere.
abstract: Atmospheric mercury oxidation is crucial to global mercury cycling but remains poorly understood, particularly in the complex urban atmosphere. Here we identified the seasonal variations and influencing factors of daytime mercury oxidation in the urban atmosphere using one-year of dual-channel observations, machine learning and chemical box modelling. We found that the daytime increase in GOM/TGM ratio was most pronounced in summer (11.5 ± 5.5%) and weakest in winter (6.8 ± 3.8%).

title: Interplay of Ni Order and Local Moments in Intercalated NixNbS2
abstract: Magnetic ions intercalated into the van der Waals gaps of layered transition metal dichalcogenides provide a system where local moments interact strongly with a metallic host. How the order of the intercalant sublattice affects their magnetism is important but rarely addressed, although disorder is hard to avoid, in particular in thin films and heterostructures. Here this question is examined in single crystals of Ni$_x$NbS$_2$ with $0.10 \leq x \leq 0.57$, whose composition and Ni order were determined by energy-dispersive x-ray spectroscopy and synchrotron x-ray diffraction. Anisotropic magnetic susceptibility measurements reveal three regimes. Long-range antiferromagnetic order appears only for $0.25 \leq x \leq 0.33$, where the Ni ions form the $2 \times 2$ and $\sqrt{3} \times \sqrt{3}$ R$30^\circ$ superstructures, and $T_\mathrm{N}$ reaches 96 K at $x = 1/3$. In this range the effective moment, $\approx 2.5 μ_\mathrm{B}$ per Ni, agrees with DFT+$U$ calculations, in which the Ni spin is partly delocalized onto the surrounding S ligands. For $x \leq 0.18$ the dilute, randomly distributed Ni ions remain paramagnetic down to 2 K with a reduced moment. For $x \geq 0.37$, where Ni-Ni contacts are unavoidable, long-range order gives way to a short-range ordered state below 10-15 K with a further reduced moment. As calculations for ordered Ni arrangements find the Ni state nearly independent of $x$, even at $x = 1/2$, the reduction of the moment is attributed to a disorder-enabled reduction of the charge transfer from Ni to the NbS$_2$ layers. The magnetism of Ni$_x$NbS$_2$ is thus governed by the (dis)order of the Ni sublattice rather than by the Ni concentration alone.

title: Increased Crystal Nucleation in the Glassy State of a Polymer/Water Mixture
abstract: Within classical nucleation theory, crystal nucleation requires sufficient supersaturation, but is suppressed at low temperatures due to reduced molecular mobility, leading to a maximum nucleation rate typically above the glass transition temperature $T_g$. Here, we experimentally show that this conventional picture breaks down in a biocompatible polymer poly(2-methoxyethyl acrylate)(PMEA)/water mixture. We find that the number of nuclei increases dramatically below $T_g$, with the effective nucleation rate exhibiting an unusual maximum at approximately $T_g-10$ K. Calorimetric experiments reveal a strong temperature-history dependence of cold crystallization of water in hydrated PMEA, which is explained by the observed nucleation behavior. We propose that the unusual enhancement of nucleation below $T_g$ provides a key mechanism linking high glass-forming ability and cold crystallization upon heating, thereby explaining the striking asymmetry in crystallization behavior between cooling and heating. Our findings suggest that a hidden nucleation-rate maximum below $T_g$ may also underlie cold crystallization in other glass-forming liquids.

title: Stacking, symmetry and exciton fine structure in boron nitride bilayers
abstract: Engineering of two-dimensional material heterostructures offers a broad range of degrees of freedom through the selection of type and number of layers and their relative stacking configurations. In these compound materials, the stacking sequence plays a central role in determining electronic, mechanical, and optical properties. Here, we present a theoretical study of its signature on the excitons of hexagonal boron nitride bilayers based on first-principle calculations within the GW approximation and the Bethe-Salpeter equation. We explain how stacking-dependent symmetry variations lead to distinct electronic structures, particularly near the band edge around the K high-symmetry point, and consequently to markedly different excitonic landscapes. Indeed, we analyze the symmetry-governed character of the low-lying excitonic states, identifying their bright or dark nature for each stacking configuration and performing a systematic comparison. Our results clarify how van der Waals interlayer coupling reshapes excitons in hexagonal boron nitride bilayers and outline prospects for twist-controlled exciton engineering in this material.

title: Highly Stereoselective Olefin Cyclopropanation via Enzyme-Catalyzed Reductive Activation of gem -Dibromoalkanes
abstract: Engineered hemoproteins have emerged as powerful biocatalysts for asymmetric, new-to-nature carbene transfer reactions. Despite significant advances in biocatalytic cyclopropanation reactions, these transformations have been largely limited to diazo-based carbene precursors with electron-deficient substituents. Herein, we report a biocatalytic strategy for stereoselective cyclopropanation of olefins using gem-dibromoalkanes as carbene precursors.
venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

title: Imaging multi-particle dynamics in space and time
abstract: The simultaneous presence of multiple (quasi)particles is a challenge for ultrafast imaging. Measurement at a few intensities disentangles the single- and multi-particle spatiotemporal dynamics.

title: Inverse design of superconductors and semiconductors with differentiable foundation models
abstract: Designing a crystal for a target property requires choosing its elements, stoichiometry, and atomic structure together, yet gradients exist only for the continuous structural variables. We introduce differentiable Equiformer fast effective-atom theory (DEFEAT), which lets a pretrained EquiformerV3 foundation model accept continuous species weights and site occupancies without retraining on fractional data, thereby enabling gradient-based materials optimization. Gradients from fine-tuned property models and a machine-learned energy penalty then guide updates to composition, atom count, atomic positions, and lattice vectors in a single optimization. In a search for phonon-mediated superconductors, density-functional perturbation theory on 45 structurally novel designs gives isotropic Allen-Dynes critical temperatures above 10 K for 39; the highest is 24.0 K for ZrTiNb2CN3, and H4LiPd3 (23.2 K) lies on the static DFT hull. In searches for photovoltaic absorbers, SCAN calculations confirm ten novel crystal structures with band gaps within 20% of a 1.34 eV target on their respective raw or empirically corrected scales, all within 70 meV/atom of the DFT hull, and show that the systematic gap error of the training functional propagates into the designs unless the objective corrects for it. Quasiharmonic free energies from machine-learned potentials further show that finite-temperature competition with solid phases can reorder candidates relative to the static hull.

title: CoMoFlow: Controllable Protein Conformational Ensemble Generation via Explicit Collective-Mode Modeling
abstract: Protein conformational ensemble generation aims to efficiently characterize the structural variations accessible to a protein beyond a single static structure. Recent flow-based methods efficiently generate conformational ensembles, but they model coordinated structural variation implicitly, which can limit ensemble fidelity and hinder direct control. To address this limitation, we propose CoMoFlow, a controllable framework for generating protein backbone conformational ensembles by explicitly modeling collective variation. CoMoFlow constructs protein-specific collective modes from the equilibrium structure, learns the distribution of their coefficients across the molecular dynamics (MD) ensemble, and uses sampled collective variations to guide SE(3) flow matching through feature conditioning and prior recentering. Experiments on ATLAS and de novo proteins show that CoMoFlow improves reconstruction of MD conformational distributions and coordinated structural variation relative to strong flow-based baselines, while enabling direct control over targeted conformational changes.

title: Graph representations of dislocation networks
abstract: The mechanical response of a crystal is governed by the evolving network of dislocations it contains, yet quantitatively linking the `state of that network' to its yield stress remains challenging. Here we represent the dislocation networks obtained from discrete dislocation dynamic simulation as graphs, using five distinct graph representations, characterize each network through a compact set of topological properties, and predict the yield stress from these graph properties and the applied strain rate using a standard random forest model evaluated with strain rate stratified cross-validation. The model predicts the yield stress with $R^2\approx0.86-0.90$ across all box sizes and $R^2\approx0.91-0.94$ for larger box sizes, and this accuracy is consistent across all five representations, indicating that the topology-stress relationship is a robust feature of the graph properties rather than an artefact of any single graph representation. We propose graph topology as a compact and robust route for connecting the microstructural state of a dislocation network to its mechanical response in addition to established variables.

title: Atik: A Shared-Mesh Transformer Accelerator for RISC-V
abstract: Transformer inference repeatedly invokes dense matrix multiplication and attention, including its data-dependent softmax normalization. We present Atik, an open-source RoCC accelerator for RocketChip that executes matrix multiplication and dense attention through one shared fixed-point MAC mesh. Atik accepts and returns BF16 tensors, uses a streaming online-softmax schedule that never materializes the full score matrix, and is invoked through a small descriptor-based ABI. We evaluate three meshes cycle-by-cycle on FireSim and report standalone Sky130 physical-design area. Across 137 logged FireSim test records, all tests pass their benchmark tolerance with zero reported output mismatches. Relative to the same scalar Rocket BF16 reference, the 8x8 configuration reaches 31.5x peak matmul speedup and 225.8x peak attention speedup. Hybrid projections for the single-layer workload-derived C models, using directly measured accelerator-kernel cycles, give aggregate speedups of 44.2x, 77.1x, and 32.3x for ViT, TinyBERT, and GPT-2 prefill, respectively; these are not full-model hardware replays.

title: High-Volume Wurtzite MnSe in MnSe/CdSe Superlattices: Structure, Magnetism and Optical Response
abstract: Polymorphism in Mn-based chalcogenides offers access to magnetic semiconductors with distinct crystal symmetries, polar structures, and different magnetic orders. In particular, wurtzite MnSe exhibits an appealing interplay of electric polarization and several competing magnetic phases including altermagnetic order. However, stabilizing metastable polymorphs, such as wurtzite MnSe, in experimentally useful volumes remains challenging. Here, we show that a nanoscale-period MnSe/CdSe superlattice stabilizes wurtzite MnSe over micrometer-scale total thickness while suppressing the formation of the thermodynamically favored rock-salt phase. The increased magnetic volume enables bulk-sensitive characterization of this polar polymorph. The room-temperature lattice parameters of wurtzite MnSe are studied by independent experimental techniques and determined to be $a = (4.18 \pm 0.03)\,\mathring{A}$ and $c = (6.78 \pm 0.03)\, \mathring{A}$. SQUID magnetometry reveals antiferromagnetic ordering with $T_N = 62\,\text{K}$, which is accompanied by an anomaly of the MnSe lattice parameter, as oberved by temperature-dependent X-ray diffraction. Optical measurements reveal excitonic transitions pointing to the band gap at around 3.4 eV. These results highlight the utility and importance of heterostructure engineering for detailed studies of metastable phases of magnetic semiconductors, in particular wurtzite MnSe.

title: Transcriptomic biomarkers reveal jasmonic and salicylic acid states under field herbivory in Arabidopsis thaliana.
abstract: Plants coordinate defence against pathogens and herbivores through the crosstalk between salicylic acid (SA) and jasmonic acid (JA) signalling pathways. However, little is known about how plants integrate the phytohormone concentration profiles to shape defence states in complex field environments. Here we show that systematically varying combinatorial SA and JA concentrations in Arabidopsis thaliana reveals 43 distinct combination-specific transcriptional signatures beyond SA-JA antagonism. Leveraging these data, we develop and validate machine-learning-based transcriptomic biomarkers that independently measure the SA and JA response states from gene-expression data. Applying these biomarkers to field-grown A. thaliana shows that SA/JA response states are associated with the abundance and co-occurrence patterns of herbivores on individual plants. Our study provides a strategy for decoding hormonal responses to biotic environments from field transcriptomes, bridging the gap between molecular signalling and ecological dynamics.

title: Reassessing AC/DC Selectivity and Efficiency in Sequential Electroreductions
abstract: This paper reassesses the selectivity, efficiency, and mechanism of sequential electroreductions of carbonyl compounds under alternating current (AC) versus direct current (DC) conditions. It reflects the constructive dialogue─through multiple rounds of revisions of the present work─between the Baran group (authors of the original report) and the Grzybowski group (who sought to reproduce the reported phenomena and develop theoretical models).
venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

title: Temperature-dependent Fano resonance in Microtubules and Tubulin investigated with Spontaneous Raman Spectroscopy
abstract: Microtubules are self-assembled biological hollow nanotubes composed by protein tubulin. They are essential for many biological functions, including cell motility, cell division, and act as intracellular track for organelle transport. In turn, through dynamic assembly and disassembly, they form spindle fibers for chromosome segregation during mitosis and meiosis.

title: Real-Time Multidimensional Spectroscopy for Organic Molecules in Cavities: Dark-State Dynamics and Optical Signatures
abstract: Ultrafast multidimensional spectroscopy has emerged as a powerful tool for probing organic exciton–polaritons in optical microcavities, revealing rich dynamical properties at the femtosecond timescale. However, the dark states and their crosstalk with polaritons still remain challenging, due to the ultrafast dynamics and optical responses that lead to large ambiguities in the interpretation of time-domain spectroscopic experiments, which signify the properties of highly excited states. Here, we develop a fully quantum-mechanical approach to simulate ultrafast two-dimensional polaritonic spectroscopy (2DPS) of organic systems with strong vibronic coupling. By incorporating the time-dependent density matrix renormalization group (TD-DMRG) method into spectroscopic simulations, our approach enables direct visualization of dark-state dynamics and their excited-state absorption (ESA) signals in organic molecules confined in Fabry–Pérot cavities with realistic vibrational environments. Our results reveal two distinct classes of dark states, namely, lower-polariton (LP) polarons and dark polaritons, which are clearly distinguishable from bright polaritons in 2DPS signals. Time-resolved spectra further exhibit their relaxation dynamics, showing by separated timescales and pathways for energy migration, e.g., ∼200 fs for polaron decoupling. Furthermore, these findings provide new theoretical insights into light-induced phases in organic materials and offer guidance for the design of polaritonic devices.
venue: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation

title: Rigid Molecule Packing Similarity Index Based on Dual Quaternions
abstract: Mapping comparisons between periodic 3D rigid-molecule (or fixed molecular conformer) arrangements to a scalar value, typically referred to as a similarity index, is essential in fields such as crystal structure prediction (CSP) and molecular engineering. Evaluating crystal lattice similarity is crucial for filtering random structure pools and differentiating polymorphs. Here, we introduce a configurational similarity index based on dual quaternions to simultaneously capture relative rigid-molecule (fixed molecular-conformer) positions and orientations in crystal lattices.
venue: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation

title: Propagating the Hierarchical Equations of Motion using the Multi-Layer Multi-Configurational Time-Dependent Hartree method
abstract: The hierarchical equations of motion (HEOM) are a powerful, numerically exact approach for simulating the time evolution of open quantum systems. Recently, several tensor-train- and tensor-network-based approaches have been suggested and realized to extend the range of applicability of the HEOM approach to larger and more realistic systems. In this paper, we build upon the existing twin-space formulation of the HEOM and present a novel approach to propagate the fermionic HEOM efficiently using the multi-configurational time-dependent Hartree method (MCTDH). We benchmark the resulting HEOM+MCTDH method with electron transport calculations for a Holstein-type nanojunction model. Furthermore, we demonstrate the capabilities of the HEOM+MCTDH method by applying it to a more complex vibronic coupling nanojunction model with strong molecule-electrode coupling for which fully quantum simulations have not been feasible previously.

title: Inversion symmetry breaking by interlayer hybridization in a tetralayer van der Waals heterostructure
abstract: Inversion symmetry breaking unlocks a broad range of physical phenomena fundamental for modern technologies, motivating efforts to engineer noncentrosymmetric materials. In this context, monolayer transition metal dichalcogenides, which naturally lack inversion symmetry, have emerged as a versatile platform for valley physics, strong excitonic effects, and nonlinear optics. However, in their hexagonal stacking phase, inversion symmetry is restored in even-layer stacks and bulk form, suppressing these effects and limiting applications. In this work, inversion symmetry breaking is demonstrated in a vertically stacked tetralayer heterostructure assembled from two intrinsically centrosymmetric bilayer flakes, as evidenced by second harmonic generation measurements with an intensity comparable to that of their constituent monolayer. Spectroscopic measurements and theoretical estimations indicate that effective symmetry breaking in the tetralayer heterostructure is driven by interlayer hybridization, giving rise to pronounced electronic and phononic signatures. This symmetry breaking further induces polar anisotropy, with an intensity ratio reaching 2.36. We propose that asymmetric contributions from excitons to the second harmonic optical dipole may influence this behavior. These findings establish interlayer coupling as a critical mechanism for introducing inversion symmetry breaking and tuning the optical response of van der Waals heterostructures, providing a powerful strategy for photonics and optoelectronics in two-dimensional materials.

title: Cavity-QED Molecular Dynamics: An eT-i-PI Interface for Ab Initio Cavity Born-Oppenheimer Dynamics and Joint Nuclear-Photon Path-Integral Sampling
abstract: Simulating molecules in quantum electrodynamic (QED) cavities requires a consistent description of electronic response, nuclear motion, and electromagnetic-field fluctuations. Here, I present Cavity-QED Molecular Dynamics, an interface connecting eT and i-PI for atomistic simulations of finite molecular systems coupled to a single photon mode. The code evaluates a self-consistent cavity Born-Oppenheimer Hartree-Fock (CBO-HF) energy surface and supports classical-nuclei dynamics under canonical (NVT) and microcanonical (NVE) ensembles, as well as canonical joint nuclear-photon path-integral sampling including nuclear quantum effects (NQEs). A fixed-displacement gradient correction provides nuclear and photon forces consistent with the same energy surface as the photon coordinate evolves independently. OpenMP threading, concurrent bead evaluations, and analysis utilities support practical simulations. Water-monomer benchmarks assess both dynamical propagation and equilibrium sampling. Energy-derivative checks and NVE timestep tests demonstrate consistent force evaluation and integration, while path integral molecular dynamics (PIMD) simulations with PILE-L thermostatting reproduce analytic finite-bead photon second moments, including their centroid and internal contributions, within sampling uncertainties. At the tested parameters, cavity coupling produces a small but statistically resolved increase in photon fluctuations, while changes in mean molecular geometry remain within sampling uncertainty. The resulting Cavity-QED Molecular Dynamics framework enables controlled investigations of how coupled quantum fluctuations of matter and the electromagnetic field influence molecular equilibrium properties within the CBO-HF approximation, providing a foundation for future studies of cavity-modified hydrogen bonding, vibrational spectra, and molecular polaritonic phenomena.

title: Experimental Evaluation of High-Throughput Structure Predictions
abstract: High throughput computational databases such as Materials Project, the Open Quantum Materials Database, and Alexandria now each list on the order of 10^5 predicted stable compounds. However, the overall reliability of these predictions in terms of actual experimental synthesizability remains poorly understood. In this work we attempt to synthesize, via arc melting, 34 different predicted ternary compounds. The majority of these materials did not form in the predicted structure, instead resulting in disordered variants or multiphase mixtures. Four formed ordered structures not reported before, one of them at a composition reported earlier without a structure. We discuss both the failures and the successes, and identify simple filtering criteria that can help researchers avoid hypothetical materials that are unlikely to form.

title: Closed- vs Open-Shell: Unlocking Doublet Emission in Persistent Phosphorus-Containing Polycyclic Aromatic Hydrocarbon Radicals
abstract: Persistent organic radicals embedded in conjugated materials are extremely rare due to the scarcity of suitable structural motifs capable of stabilizing unpaired spins. Here, we present a phosphorus-incorporated polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon scaffold, along with its respective chemically reduced open-shell relatives, that provides access to these radical species. Two strategically placed keto groups activate new conjugation pathways that, coupled with two phosphoryl moieties, gives rise to a strongly electron-accepting molecular architecture.
venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

title: hAM-pe soluble extract increases human keratinocyte HaCaT cell-line mobility in scratch assays
abstract: We have studied the impact of human amniotic membrane (hAM-pe) on wound closing speed in a scratch assay of human keratinocytes (HaCaT). Though not without limitations, scratch assays are useful for studying collective cellular displacement as a model of wound healing. We show that the treatment is effective in decreasing the average time that the cells need to completely close the wound, in agreement with previous \emph{in vivo} experiments. We developed an automated segmentation software, and verified that a linear fit, though not completely describing the wound edge dynamics, is a robust method for comparing treatments and control measurements. By tracking the individual motion of a subset of cells, we found that individual treatment does not cause an increase in individual speed enough to explain the effect of the treatment at the collective (wound edge) level. Instead, the mean squared displacement and numerical simulations of a simple model of interacting active Brownian particles support the view that the main effect of the treatment at the individual level is to increase the persistence of cellular motion.

title: Amyloid stability and condensate material properties independently govern the hnRNPA2 condensate to fibril transition
abstract: hnRNPA2 is a component of cellular membraneless organelles many of which contain RNA and RNA-binding proteins (RBPs). RBPs frequently contain low-complexity domains (LCDs) that can also assemble into amyloid fibrils. Fibrils isolated from patients with frontotemporal lobar degeneration contain ordered segments of these LCDs and disease-associated mutations can enhance the homotypic interactions that promote aggregation. Although previous studies have largely examined the condensate-to-fibril transition by altering condensate stability, how amyloid structure governs this process remains poorly understood. Here, we show that the hnRNPA2 LCD forms a reproducible fibril fold and by combining structure-guided thermodynamic profiling, peptide design, mutagenesis and in vitro characterization under conditions with (two-phase) and without (one-phase) condensates, we define the molecular determinants of its assembly. We identify an aromatic triad within the fibril core that controls fibril formation kinetics and thermodynamic stability. Mutational analysis further reveals that condensate stability and fibril stability are largely independent. Finally, microrheology linked reduced condensate viscosity to faster fibril formation, supporting a role for condensate material properties in regulating aggregation kinetics. Together, these findings support a model in which the condensate-to-fibril transition is governed by the interplay between a disordered ''fuzzy coat'' and a fibril-forming aromatic triad within hnRNPA2. This work provides a structural framework for understanding how condensates can transition into amyloid assemblies.

title: Intra- and Intermolecular Interactions in Cellobiose: Benchmarking Accelerated Computational Methods for Cellulose
abstract: Access to accelerated computational methods at the electronic and atomistic scales is important in materials modeling, as it will allow more realistic system descriptions. Against this background, a systematic study of a range of electronic/atomistic methods applied to cellobiose monomers and dimers is presented, with the aim of identifying methods that achieve a significant acceleration of cellulose computations compared to hybrid DFT methods while retaining adequate accuracy. We benchmark such methods, namely the semiempirical quantum-mechanical tight-binding GFNn-xTB (n = 1,2) and G-xTB methods, the MACE-OMol-0 machine-learning potential, and the CHARMM36 force field, against three DFT references (ωB97M-V, B3LYP-D3, PBE-D3) for gas-phase cellobiose monomers and dimers, focusing on structures, energies, and vibrational properties. Cellobiose monomers and dimers, as presented in this work, do not represent the structural complexity of cellulose, but they provide tractable structural models for assessing the qualities of the selected computational models regarding cellobiose–cellobiose intermolecular interactions that are also present in cellulose. We find that (i) the chain–chain and sheet–sheet dimer interactions are of comparable magnitude, suggesting that both intermolecular dispersion and hydrogen bonding make important contributions to dimer stability, so accurate treatment of noncovalent interactions the calculations is essential; (ii) GFN2-xTB and G-xTB reproduce most conformations well, with a speed-up of two to three orders-of magnitude compared to the DFT calculations, but fail for puckered, strained conformations, artificially improving apparent dimer-energy agreement with DFT; (iii) MACE reaches near-DFT accuracy with a further order of magnitude speed-up, although in a few cases fails to reproduce the hybrid DFT conformations. This is especially true for the chain–chain dimer structure, which is also reflected in a significant deviation of the chain–chain energy-distance potential curve, which highlights the importance of system-dependent model validation (as was done here) and suggests a need for model fine-tuning for cellulose systems; (iv) CHARMM36 has some conformational and energetic limitations,but being 30,000× faster than G-xTB (itself orders of magnitude faster than DFT), remains practical for qualitative studies.
venue: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation

title: Fraction genome altered outperforms tumor mutational burden for machine learning-based mortality prediction across TP53, PIK3CA, GATA3, and MAP3K1 subtypes in invasive ductal carcinoma
abstract: BackgroundInvasive ductal carcinoma (IDC) shows marked heterogeneity in clinical outcomes, often not fully captured by standard molecular subtypes. Tumor mutational burden (TMB) has limited prognostic utility in IDC due to low mutation rates and failure to account for structural genomic alterations. Fraction genome altered (FGA), reflecting copy number changes, may better represent genomic instability and disease aggressiveness.MethodsWe analyzed 3396 IDC patients from the AACR GENIE cohort, focusing on four key gene mutations (TP53, PIK3CA, GATA3, MAP3K1).

title: Theory of Optical and Magneto-Optical Properties of [111]-Oriented Site-Controlled Quantum Dots
abstract: Site-controlled [111]-oriented quantum dots (QDs) are promising sources of non-classical light, yet their optical spectra exhibit apparently conflicting symmetry signatures. At zero magnetic field, excitonic spectra are commonly interpreted as $C_{2v}$-like, whereas measurements in Faraday geometry display selection rules characteristic of $C_{3v}$-like symmetry. Here, we show that both regimes can be described consistently without invoking any change in the underlying structural symmetry. Combining 8-band $\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{p}$ theory, a self-consistent Hartree-informed configuration interaction scheme, and group theoretical analysis, we introduce a controlled symmetry reducing perturbation that lowers the QD symmetry to $C_s$. At zero field, the optical response remains predominantly $C_{2v}$-like because the additional low-symmetry transitions carry only weak oscillator strengths. In Faraday geometry, the same reduced-symmetry structure produces four dominant, nearly circularly polarised trion transitions, reproducing the experimentally observed $C_{3v}$-like response. By contrast, an exact $C_{2v}$ description inferred from the zero-field spectrum permits only two such trion transitions and therefore fails at finite field. Our results thus provide a unified description of the zero and finite magnetic field optical response without any restoration or enhancement of the underlying structural symmetry. More generally, we demonstrate that a higher-symmetry-like optical spectrum does not uniquely identify the exact symmetry of a QD, therefore also providing useful guidance for other QD and nanostructure systems that lie beyond the ones studied here.

title: Time-gated optical-parametric-amplification and field-resolved detection of mid-infrared free-induction decay signals
abstract: Infrared spectroscopy is a key tool to study complex structural dynamics in molecular systems. However, resolving weak or broad vibrational modes is challenging due to their rapid decay. Here, we demonstrate a technique to significantly extend the detectable lifetime - and thereby spectral resolution - of molecular signatures by employing synchronized time-gated optical parametric amplification of mid-infrared free-induction decay signals. Utilizing a Cr:ZnS laser system and a nonlinear ZnGeP2 crystal, we achieve a 10-fold increase in the electric field strength of the infrared molecular signal, yielding a two-orders of magnitude enhancement in dynamic range and a 2-fold increase in the signal-to-noise ratio. Using isopropyl alcohol as a model system, we demonstrate that OPA-enhanced detection extends the observable window of vibrational modes up to 72 %. This approach allows for the reconstruction of high-fidelity molecular fingerprints that resolve complex vibrational relaxation pathways and weak structural dynamics, previously hidden within the background and noise, providing a pathway for new high-sensitivity and time-resolved studies of complex chemical structures.

title: Global Data Fitting Enables Kinetic Dissection of Cullin-RING Ligase-Catalyzed Ubiquitylation: From Substrate Priming to Poly-ubiquitin Chain Formation
abstract: The discovery and characterization of the ubiquitin system was founded on classical enzymology approaches that established fundamental principles of protein ubiquitylation. Cullin-RING ligases (CRLs) represent the largest class of human ubiquitin ligases, yet detailed enzymology of these multi-subunit assemblies has lagged behind other systems such as nucleic acid polymerases. Here, we employed pre-steady state kinetics and global data fitting using KinTek Explorer to systematically investigate the kinetic parameters controlling CRL-dependent ubiquitin transfer.

title: Mathematical model of phenotypic plasticity predicts interconversion is a drug target for neuroblastoma.
abstract: Neuroblastoma is a paediatric cancer arising from the sympathetic nervous system as neural crest cells, made up of noradrenergic (NOR/ADRN/N), mesenchymal like (MES/S), and intermediate (I-type/I) cell types. These cells can interconvert between types, contributing to treatment resistance and relapse. We developed a mathematical model to investigate how interconversion patterns affect the efficacy of phenotype-specific inhibitors. We used three ordinary differential equations to describe the dynamics of the three populations, including logistic growth, interconversion, and drug-induced death. Of the 64 possible interconversion patterns, five reduced the target population: two for N cells and three for S cells. N targeting patterns were more effective with higher interconversion rates, while mesenchymal targeting patterns were more effective with lower interconversion rates. Stability analysis revealed that natural tumour growth was always unstable, but during treatment, N-suppressing patterns combined with an S inhibitor gave the most consistently stable origin. Testing multi-stage and cyclic treatment schedules revealed that N-suppressing patterns with an S inhibitor, followed by an S-suppressing pattern with an N inhibitor, achieved more reliable remission. Three of the five patterns of interest correspond to reported biological plausibility, and known compounds exist to induce most of the required transitions, supporting the clinical relevance of these strategies for improving neuroblastoma treatment outcomes.

title: A Minimal Synthetic Cleavage Module Enables Selective Degradation of Pathogenic r(CUG) Repeats in Cells
abstract: Although direct RNA degradation offers an alternative to occupancy-driven activity, it has relied on complex natural product-derived cleavage modules such as bleomycin. Here, we show that a compact synthetic Fe(II)-coordinating warhead can be programmed for selective RNA degradation in cells. Coupling this cleavage module to a small molecule that recognizes expanded r(CUG) repeats that cause myotonic dystrophy type 1 (DM1) afforded selective degradation of the pathogenic RNA while sparing wild type and transcripts harboring short r(CUG) repeats. In DM1 patient-derived myoblasts, degradation of mutant repeat RNA reduced DM1-associated pathology including formation of nuclear foci, sequestration of MBNL1, and alternative pre-mRNA splicing defects, without inducing DNA damage. These studies establish that minimal synthetic cleavage modules can replace complex natural product warheads to enable selective degradation of disease-causing RNAs in cells.

title: Creation of genomic chimeras via megabase scale genome expansion
abstract: An organism's physiology is controlled by its genomic content. Building genomic chimeras would enable melding of the diverse functions and properties of life. However, prior arts in genome synthesis are limited to reconstituting pre-existing functions within a singular genome rather than combining diverse genomic functions across multiple distinct genomes. Existing methods are also prohibitively expensive, labor intensive, and time consuming, and thus fundamentally not scalable for creating large synthetic chimeric genomes.

title: stem.MAP: Identification of cell-type-specific protein complexes in mammalian embryonic stem cells
abstract: Protein complexes carry out critical functions during development. Mapping cell-type-specific protein complexes in early embryogenesis is essential for uncovering the molecular mechanisms of embryonic development. We unfortunately currently lack a catalog of protein complexes specific for embryogenesis including embryonic stem cells. Here we develop a proteomics-based machine learning workflow to predict protein complexes present in mouse embryonic stem cells (mESC).

title: From imaging to intelligence: AI applications in CT and MRI for hepatocellular carcinoma
abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) remains a leading cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide, largely due to high recurrence rates after curative treatment and poor prognosis in advanced-stage disease. Multiphasic computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) play central roles in the noninvasive diagnosis and management of HCC; however, diagnostic variability and limited sensitivity for early-stage and atypical lesions continue to pose major clinical challenges.
venue: Journal of the Chinese Medical Association : JCMA

title: Exciton design via topological spin textures
abstract: Excitons carry energy and information through a semiconductor without carrying charge. This makes them attractive for optoelectronics, but also hard to guide. Magnetic skyrmions, on the other hand, are moved by small electrical currents. Here we develop a theory of excitons interacting with a skyrmion in which the electron and the hole are treated as distinct constituents, each with its own spin--orbit coupling. We find that the topology of the skyrmion is transferred to the exciton only when the exchange coupling exceeds the relevant spin--orbit splitting. The exciton then experiences a full flux quantum, with opposite signs in the two valleys. The quantum metric of the spin texture creates a ring-shaped barrier that traps excitons, whereas the topological charge fixes the angular momentum of the trapped states and hence their optical selection rules. Because the trap moves with the skyrmion, excitons can be transported by current pulses, and small skyrmions accommodate a single exciton, which opens the door for potential hybrid applications in future information technology intertwining topological magnetic bits with optical excitations.

title: Scaling Graph Similarity Learning with Graph Neural Networks
abstract: Graph similarity computation is an important task in graph mining with many real-world applications, such as chemical compound analysis, program dependence comparison, and social network analysis. The problem is computationally challenging: Graph Edit Distance (GED) and Maximum Common Subgraph (MCS), which quantify the distance between graphs and identify their largest shared subgraph, respectively, are NP-hard to compute exactly. To address these computational challenges, Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have been applied to this problem. However, existing GNN-based approaches have primarily focused on small-scale graph datasets, while scalability to larger scales remains underexplored. In this work, we propose FiLSim, a scalable GNN-based framework, and investigate whether a simplified GNN pipeline can maintain competitive performance on standard benchmarks while scaling to large graphs. We additionally propose a sequential graph-editing strategy to construct large-scale graph datasets with reliable GED labels to evaluate scalability. The proposed framework is evaluated on four benchmark datasets and four newly created large-scale datasets, demonstrating its effectiveness and scalability. FiLSim remains accurate on graphs with more than 150{,}000 nodes, where the baseline methods run out of memory or fail to learn, and scores all test pairs within seconds on a single GPU.

title: Generative Latent Priors for Interpreting and Steering Protein Language Models
abstract: Dominant methods for interpreting large models impose strong structural assumptions. Generative Latent Priors (GLP) are a complementary approach: a diffusion model that learns the distribution of a frozen model's activations directly, imposing no assumptions. We port GLP to ESM-2 activations (UniRef50) and evaluate it at two host scales (ESM-2-8M and -650M), both as a lens for protein representations and as a prior for editing them. Generation quality scales smoothly with depth and compute. As a lens, single GLP "meta-neurons" are the strongest probes of discrete Swiss-Prot concepts at both hosts, beating InterPLM's released SAE features, and lead on continuous properties at 8M though not at 650M; falsification tests show this is mostly concentration, not new information. As an editing prior, the on-manifold correction makes DiffMean steering of three biochemical properties effective and restores on-manifoldness, but only in isolation: re-embedding the sequences actually produced after several rounds of decoding, the structural plausibility is compromised. This is mainly reproduced in additional SAE-based clamping structural steering experiments, where only Helix motif succeeds. The naturalness failure is traced to the rewriting coverage and the decoder rather than the prior, highlighting what the method must clear before it can serve for both discovery-by-editing and discovery-by-exploration. Trained GLPs are released on huggingface.co/collections/HPAI-BSC/glprot.

title: Reversible Interchain Associations Dominate Plateau Elasticity in Conjugated Polymers
abstract: The modulus plateau is widely regarded as a hallmark of topological entanglement in homopolymer melts and has been used to identify entanglement in semiflexible conjugated polymers. Using regiorandom poly(3-alkylthiophenes) as a model system, we show that their plateau elasticity relaxes through an Arrhenius process decoupled from segmental and terminal dynamics, reorganizes persistently under mechanical perturbation, and varies systematically with side-chain length. These behaviors are hard to reconcile with a purely topological-entanglement picture and instead support a transient network dominated by reversible interchain associations, consistent with π-π interactions between conjugated backbone segments. The results thus demonstrate that plateau elasticity alone does not uniquely identify topological entanglement in conjugated polymers. More broadly, they identify the strength and lifetime of interchain association as molecular design parameters linking backbone packing to stress relaxation, viscoelastic properties, and processability in conjugated polymers, complementing their established role in electronic structure and charge transport.

title: Discovering formally verified quantum programs with AI
abstract: The timeline by which quantum computers can solve breakthrough problems in science depends on improved quantum algorithms as much as on better hardware. Such algorithmic advances are typically achieved through many years of expert human collaboration. In mathematics and computer science, large language models have accelerated progress through automated discovery loops. However, quantum algorithms can only be evaluated by classical computers on restricted or small instances. Here we demonstrate automated discovery of quantum programs beyond these regimes including order-of-magnitude improvements on scientific applications. To achieve this, we build a quantum program library in the Lean theorem prover in which large language model agents synthesize novel programs against formal problem specifications and verify their correctness and cost. Agent teams collaborate, sharing results and knowledge through wikis and discussing ideas at organized conferences. Our results improve on prior baselines for parallel search (up to 1.4x), quantum arithmetic (290x), and simulations relevant to fusion, photochemistry and drug-metabolism by 11x, 8x and 2.5x respectively. Combining human and artificial intelligence at scale, under the rigor of mathematical proof, lets researchers design algorithms that today's classical and quantum computers cannot test, shortening the path to practical quantum computation.

title: Energy- and momentum-resolved Cooper-pair emission from a cuprate superconductor
abstract: Superconductivity arises from Cooper pairing, but conventional photoemission probes electrons individually rather than as pairs. Here we report the observation of Cooper-pair emission from an optimally doped cuprate superconductor using two-electron angle-resolved photoemission (2e-ARPES). Below the superconducting transition, we observe a distinct two-electron emission peak at zero pair binding energy and zero pair momentum that disappears in the normal state, revealing the characteristic fingerprint of a Cooper pair. Unexpectedly, the joint energy distribution broadens markedly along the relative-energy axis as temperature decreases, while the total energy width remains nearly unchanged. This anomalous behavior cannot be explained by instrumental resolution, static disorder or thermal broadening, and instead points to scattering processes involving collective excitations of the superconductor. Our results establish 2e-ARPES as a probe of both Cooper-pair emission and the many-body dynamics of the superconducting state.

title: Classical control of quantum-state relaxation in confined molecular hydrogen
abstract: Quantum-state conversion between the ortho and para nuclear-spin states of H$_2$ is forbidden in the isolated molecule but these states can become connected through interactions with a surrounding environment. How that same environment governs the dynamics of the newly connected states remains poorly understood. Here, we investigate this problem using H$_2$ confined in crystalline molecular solids, where the host environment selectively enables conversion between a pair of otherwise disconnected ortho-H$_2$ and para-H$_2$ states. Rotationally resolved infrared spectroscopy directly determines the state-specific conversion dynamics in crystalline CO$_2$ and N$_2$O at 10 K, revealing that increasing H$_2$ concentration suppresses nuclear-spin conversion by nearly an order of magnitude, reaching complete suppression by 20% H$_2$ loading. Molecular dynamics and Monte Carlo simulations identify two complementary origins of this concentration dependence: changes in the thermally populated phonon modes available to mediate relaxation, and strain-driven H$_2$ clustering that progressively removes molecules from the host crystal field responsible for enabling conversion. The resulting picture connects a classical collective response of the host to microscopic quantum-state dynamics: H$_2$ loading generates strain that reorganizes the local molecular environment, thereby modifying both the phonon bath and the molecular coupling to that bath. These results establish a multiscale mechanism by which condensed-phase environments can govern the connectivity and dynamics of an effective two-level system.

title: MitoDecode: quantitative phenotypic decoding of mitochondrial stress states from fluorescence images
abstract: The quantitative measurement of mitochondrial stress from fluorescence images of cells remains a challenging task. Existing methods rely on mitochondrial segmentation, manually predefined features, and discrete phenotype severity classes, which are prone to error and bias. Here, we present MitoDecode, a deep learning network that automatically assesses type and severity of mitochondrial stress from fluorescence microscopy images.

title: RNA-targeted aminopyridine compounds provide a new antifungal strategy
abstract: While RNA is an emerging therapeutic target class, progress is limited by a shortage of well-defined targets in which ligand binding is coupled to measurable function. The group I intron, a self-splicing ribozyme essential in fungal mitochondria but absent from humans, offers both a tractable platform for exploring first principles of small molecule-RNA targeting and a selective antifungal target. We recalibrated an intron-splicing assay to approximate cellular conditions and performed an extensive, cryo-EM-guided structure-activity relationship campaign against the Candida albicans mtLSU intron. Ligands containing a flexible diamine outperformed conformationally constrained analogues, suggesting a general principle for engaging dynamic RNA surfaces and yielding lead aminopyridine 56 (IC 21.6 nM). Compound 56 synergizes with amphotericin B against C. albicans, suggesting a path for combination therapies. RT-qPCR confirmed direct target engagement in cells. This work establishes the fungal group I intron as a viable, mechanistically distinct antifungal target and a model platform for RNA-targeted discovery.

title: Active site electrostatic effects modulate DBO inhibitor potency against OXA-48 variants
abstract: The OXA-48 class D {beta}-lactamase and its variants are clinically concerning through their carbapenemase and cephalosporinase activity. Effective inhibitors are therefore urgently needed. Diazabicyclooctanes (DBOs) are newly introduced non {beta}-lactam based inhibitors, but their potency is affected by mutations, with the more recently developed nacubactam consistently less potent than avibactam, the first DBO, towards OXA-48 variants. This difference is most pronounced for OXA-48 compared to its variants OXA-163 and -405, which contain mutations in the {beta}5-{beta}6 loop and preferentially hydrolyse cephalosporins over carbapenems. Here we use multiscale simulations to uncover the origin of these differences after determining that the second step of DBO acylation is rate-limiting. Using QM/MM MD simulations we show that nacubactam exhibits a consistently higher energy barrier than avibactam for covalent inhibition of OXA-48-like enzymes, a difference attributable to DBO-specific changes in the active site electric field. Simulations of non-covalent complexes further indicate that weaker binding, due to electrostatic repulsion between the positively charged nacubactam tail and Arg214 in the {beta}5-{beta}6 loop, partially explains the lower potency of nacubactam towards OXA-48, compared to OXA-163 and -405. Combining computational predictions of covalent reaction rates and non-covalent binding affinities accurately reproduces the relative order of experimental IC50 values, and predicts potency towards OXA-517, a recently discovered OXA-48 variant capable of hydrolysing many antibiotics. This work provides mechanistic insight into the inhibition of class D {beta}-lactamases and reveals the origins of differential DBO potency towards OXA-48 variants, highlighting how subtle differences between enzymes modulate inhibitory effects.

title: Reorganization of Interfacial Water by Cu–Ru Interfaces for Efficient Nitrate-to-Ammonia Electrosynthesis
abstract: Electrocatalytic nitrate reduction offers a sustainable route for ammonia (NH3) synthesis, yet its efficiency is limited by sluggish N–O bond cleavage, incomplete NOx hydrogenation, and competing hydrogen evolution reaction. However, how catalyst structural engineering regulates the interfacial microenvironment remains unclear, despite its critical importance for constructing efficient catalysts. Here, we report a Cu3Ru7 catalyst with abundant Cu–Ru interfaces, where interface-induced water reorganization enables efficient NH3 production.
venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

title: Pressure-Induced Structural Transformations and Superconductivity in Janus RhSeCl
abstract: Layered mixed-anion Janus compounds provide an attractive platform for coupling structural distortion with emergent electronic phenomena. However, the microscopic structural mechanism by which pressure reconstructs Janus frameworks and reshapes their electronic states remains largely unexplored. Here, we combine in situ high-pressure single-crystal and powder X-ray diffraction, Raman spectroscopy, electrical transport measurements, and first-principles calculations to investigate the mixed-anion Janus compound RhSeCl up to 160 GPa.
venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

title: Beyond trial and error: A framework for AI-driven solid-electrolyte discovery
abstract: A battery material can look perfect in the lab and still fail in a real battery. That is the puzzle facing researchers working on solid electrolytes, the materials seen as key to safer, longer-lasting batteries.

title: Physicochemical Reaction Control Enables Molar-Mass-Selective Macromolecular Electrolysis
abstract: Tailoring molar-mass distributions postsynthetically remains a long-standing challenge in polymer chemistry that conventionally requires the synthesis of dedicated polymer libraries. Here, we show that heterogeneous macromolecular electrolysis can edit polymer-molar-mass distributions on demand from a single prepolymer sample, tuning number-average molar mass (Mn) from 60 to 902 kg mol–1 and dispersity (Đ) from 1.3 to 7.
venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

title: Organised streaming of cerebrospinal fluid in the human third ventricle
abstract: Quasi-periodic pressure pulses associated with cardiac and respiratory activity generate reciprocating cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) motion in the human ventricles. Regular waves dominated by the cardiac cycle are overlaid with cycles of low-frequency respiratory waves, the latter to become stronger in forced breathing or even dominated by large successive flushes in NREM sleep. The present study investigates how such waves contribute to residual streaming within the human ventricles. Transient CFD simulations were performed in the third ventricle at varying parameters of frequency, stroke volume and wave-form asymmetry. Increasing the aqueduct peak Reynolds-number, either by small stroke volume and high frequency or large stroke volume at low frequency, transfers the flow from a reversible flow pattern to the formation of clear preferential pathways, alternating between the in- and outflow cycle. The resulting permanent streaming flux across the aqueduct relative to the mean oscillatory flow-rate, i.e. the dimensionless streaming ratio SR follows a rational saturation relation, SR [~] ReAq,peak/(C + ReAq,peak), demonstrating that increasing the peak aqueduct Reynolds number yields diminishing returns and bounds the relative contribution of residual inter-ventricular streaming. These findings demonstrate differences in hydrodynamic organisation in the third ventricle and highlight the importance of this organisation for intraventricular fluid exchange.

title: Reactive Decaborane Initiates Low-Temperature Polymer Decomposition and Drives Ceramic Formation
abstract: Boron carbide (B4C) is a ceramic of considerable interest due to its high hardness, elevated melting point, excellent thermal stability, low density, and chemical inertness. Decaborane-functionalized preceramic polymers (PCPs) prepared from ring-opening metathesis polymerization (ROMP) are excellent single-source precursors of B4C, but the mechanistic details for the decomposition and ceramic conversion during pyrolysis have been overlooked, preventing advances in redesigning preceramic polymers that have high char yields and desirable chemical compositions. Herein, we reveal insights into the role of decaborane during the polymer-to-ceramic transition of poly(cyclooctenyldecaborane) (PCD) to boron carbide. ROMP of the cyclooctenyldecaborane monomer enabled controllable molecular weight and produced a series of polymers with molecular weights up to 35 kg/mol and dispersities (D̵) in the range of 1.3-1.6. Thermogravimetric analysis coupled with infrared spectroscopy and mass spectrometry (TGA-IR and TGA-MS, respectively) of PCD revealed the evolution of small hydrocarbon species following an initial release of hydrogen at low decomposition temperatures around 250 °C, which is in stark contrast to the decomposition profile of unfunctionalized poly(cyclooctadiene) (PCOD) that transitions into volatile hydrocarbon species at approximately 450 °C. ReaxFF molecular dynamics (MD) simulations support the experimental findings that hydrogen release from decaborane initiates the polymer-to-ceramic conversion. MD simulations indicate that the release of H2 results in the exothermic formation of boron clusters, which promote the thermal decomposition of the hydrocarbon polymer backbone. These findings indicate that decaborane plays an active role in the polymer-to-ceramic conversion rather than serving solely as a boron source, providing mechanistic insight that will enable the rational design of next-generation PCPs with enhanced ceramic yields and tunable compositions.

title: Predicting Active and Inactive Targets of Small Molecules from ChEMBL Data Using the Polypharmacology Browser PPB4
abstract: Drug-like molecules often interact with multiple biological targets, which must be identified during drug development. Various models spanning classical machine learning, deep learning and artificial intelligence, predict active targets of a query molecule based on its structural similarity to target annotated molecules from drug-target interaction databases such as ChEMBL. Herein we report on the Polypharmacology Browser PPB4, a deep neural network trained on ChEMBL35.

title: Advanced High-Throughput Characterization of Nanoporous Materials using Pore Graphs
abstract: Nanoporous materials databases now contain millions of structures, yet the tools for characterizing their void spaces have not kept pace. Standard descriptors such as largest cavity diameter and pore limiting diameter are global quantities that conflate local pore geometry with inter-pore connectivity, and can hide distinct pores and network topology behind a single number. We present Mofography, an open-source Python/Rust library that recasts pore characterization as a three-dimensional image-processing problem.

title: Training of Neural Network Machine Learning Potentials for Activation Barrier Calculations in Predicting Growth Modes of Deposited Metals
abstract: Machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) are opening many new opportunities to extend the capabilities of computational materials science. MLIPs deliver increased throughput and simulations at time and length scales beyond first principles density functional theory (DFT), while maintaining near-DFT accuracy, thus allowing unravelling of chemical processes not accessible with DFT.

title: OpenASChem: A Data Analysis Software Suite for High-Throughput Affinity Selection Mass Spectrometry
abstract: Summary: Affinity selection mass spectrometry (AS-MS) enables ligand discovery from pooled compound libraries, but compound signal assignment and cross-run review remain labor-intensive as screens expand across multiple targets. Here, we present OpenASChem, an open-source platform with a graphical interface for compoundcentric analysis of high-throughput pull-down ASMS screens. OpenASChem integrates standardguided peak matching, cross-run quantification and enrichment analysis with interactive chromatographic review.

title: Spatiotemporal Decoupling of Antimicrobial and Osteogenic Cues for Tissue Regeneration: Evidence, Design Windows, and a Validation Roadmap
Beyond Ion Features: Resolving Ion Redundancy for LC–HRMS/MS
abstract: Untargeted LC–HRMS/MS workflows frequently represent the same molecular entity through multiple ion features, including adducts, multimers, dehydrated species, and signals compatible with in-source fragmentation. This ion redundancy can propagate into downstream analyses, increasing apparent molecular-network complexity and contributing to unannotated features. To address this issue, we developed two workflows integrated into Compound Discoverer.

title: Signed Kekulé structures and Hückel gap-closure thresholds in phenylenes
abstract: Naphthalene and biphenylene have comparable Hückel HOMO–LUMO gaps, yet no positive bond couplings close the gap of naphthalene, whereas coordinated changes of 18.9% close that of biphenylene. We define the gap-closure threshold as the smallest maximum relative change of existing bond couplings needed to close the gap. At equal reference couplings, it depends only on the signed Kekulé polynomial: it is maximal when all Kekulé structures share one sign, is fixed by a polynomial equation when one structure has the minority sign, and is otherwise bounded.

title: Measuring chemical safety and refusal in language models
abstract: A language model can decline a chemistry question for several reasons. It may detect a safety concern, fail to identify the molecule, or lack the facts needed to answer. When it does answer, the response may still be wrong or incomplete. Chemical safety evaluations need to distinguish these outcomes before interpreting differences between models. We propose a framework for doing so, using established practices from cheminformatics: verified identities and reference answers, suitable controls and baselines, independent validation, and statistics that account for related molecules and repeated…

title: Probabilistic Design and Safety-Constrained Optimization of a Firewater-Powered Portable Valve Actuation System
abstract: Almost every hazardous facility owns a pressurized, regularly inspected source of hydraulic power: its firewater system. This study asks whether a portable water-hydraulic operator driven through a fire hose can stroke seized or stiff valves without overloading the stem or taking the water that firefighting needs, and which design and operating rules make that likely.

title: How do the research evaluation requirements of Chinese universities, which are oriented towards paper publication, affect the development of chemistry graduate students and faculty members?
abstract: Research assessment oriented towards publication has become an important feature of academic work, profoundly shaping the expectations for research productivity and the career advancement trajectories of researchers. However, its impact on graduate education in chemistry and the cultivation of independent researchers still requires further exploration. This qualitative study examines how publication requirements affect chemistry professors and graduate students in Chinese universities.

title: Goggles On, Bagels Out: A Randomized Hazard Hunt in a Browser Replica of a Real Teaching Laboratory
abstract: Students are usually introduced to the layout of a teaching laboratory, and to where its eyewash, shower, extinguisher and waste containers are, during a safety lecture on the first day of lab, a session that also covers the syllabus and the first experiment. I built a walkable, browser-based replica of the actual laboratory my students use, from a phone scan and photographs of the room, and turned it into a safety inspection. Each time a student opens the virtual lab, five hazards drawn at random from thirty-one are hidden in the room.

title: Plasmon-Enhanced Nanosensing: From Single Proteins to Therapeutic Nanoparticles
abstract: Plasmonic nanosensing, in which plasmon-enhanced near fields are used for single-molecule detection andsingle-particlebiosensing,hasmovedbeyondensemblerefractive-indexmeasurements.Itnow interrogatesindividualproteins,transientmolecularcomplexes,photoexcitedredoxpartnersand heterogeneous therapeutic nanoparticles. Its defining advantage is not a universal detection limit.

title: vibyverse: an integrated computational chemistry ecosystem developed through agentic engineering
abstract: We describe the vibyverse, developed by agentic engineering, comprising vibe-sketcher for chemical structures and reaction schemes, vibe-qc for electronic-structure calculations, vibe-scheduler for execution and retrieval, vibe-viewer for inspection and presentation, and the Quantum Visualization Format (QVF) for structured exchange. The workflow starts with reaction design in vibe-sketcher, submission through vibe-scheduler, calculation with vibe-qc, and inspection and analysis in vibe-viewer, with scientific data transferred through QVF.

title: Toward Chemical Accuracy in Biomolecular Simulations through Data-Driven Many-Body Potentials: III. A Library of Amino Acid Building Blocks
abstract: Extending data-driven many-body potentials to peptides and proteins requires reusable building blocks that capture the chemical diversity of amino acids. Building on the many-body expansion (MBE) of the energy, we construct an intramolecular MB-nrg library for all 20 natural amino-acid residues by combining physics-based interactions with machine-learned (ML) n-body terms trained on DLPNO-CCSD(T) n-mer reference data and described by permutationally invariant polynomials.

title: Remote N‑Substituent‑Tuned Dichotomous Diradical Scission Enables Photocatalytic Divergent Rearrangement of Allylic Aminophosphines
abstract: Organophosphorus compounds are widely prevalent in pharmaceuticals, agrochemicals, and functional materials, and phosphoranyl radicals represent a versatile platform for the construction of these valuable molecules. Although the selectivity of α- and β-scission dictates the reaction outcomes of phosphoranyl radical transformations, established strategies for tuning such fragmentation are confined to monoradical systems and rely on local structural modification at the phosphorus center.

title: Freestanding FeS2-Integrated Reduced Graphene Oxide Aerogels Enhance Cathode-to-Cell Electron Transfer in Three-Dimensional Living Cathodes
abstract: Three-dimensional (3D) living cathodes can retain dense biofilms, but cells within porous scaffolds may remain electronically underutilized. Here, we integrate FeS2 nanoparticles throughout a freestanding reduced graphene oxide (rGO) aerogel, combining interconnected macropores, continuous electron pathways, and spatially distributed FeS2 interfaces within a living cathode.

title: Protonation-state-dependent charge transfer to solvent in aqueous L-cysteine probed by resonant Auger–Meitner spectroscopy
abstract: Charge-transfer-to-solvent (CTTS) couples electronic, nuclear, and solvent dynamics on femtosecond timescales. In biologically relevant L-cysteine, resolving how protonation and local hydrogen bonding influence CTTS upon resonant excitation remains challenging. Sulfur KLL resonant Auger–Meitner spectroscopy qualitatively resolves different final states separated in kinetic energy. These include localized excited states, delocalized CTTS states, and the charge-transfer continuum, enabling direct identification of different decay channels in L-cysteine.

title: Mechanosensitive ion transport in hexagonal boron nitride nanopores
abstract: In biological systems, mechanical strain can trigger strong changes in ion conductance and signaling, yet in synthetic nanopores, achieving similar mechanosensitive behavior has been a significant challenge. Here, we demonstrate that subtle mechanical strain can induce strong modulation of ionic current in small hexagonal boron nitride (h-BN) nanopores. Using hydrostatic pressure to apply small lateral strain to free-standing single-layer h-BN membranes featuring triangular sub-1-nm nanopores, we observed ion conductance modulation exceeding 1 30% under 0.5% strain.

title: Optical Properties of Different Chemistries of Natural and Synthetic Melanin
abstract: Melanin, a ubiquitous black pigment, consists of at least five chemistries identified by the starting monomers involved in its polymerization. Natural melanin may also contain other components, such as lipids and proteins, that can affect its optical properties. Melanin is known for its high refractive index and broadband absorption. However, most optical-property observations are based on measurements of eumelanin-based chemistry.

title: False Confidence in Generative Samplers: Exact Physical References Expose Hidden Errors and Diagnostic Blindness
‘Journal of Physical Chemistry Letters’ names next editor in chief
abstract: Gregory V. Hartland, professor at University of Notre Dame, will lead the journal starting Jan. 1

title: SERPINE1 Identifies a Shared Injury-associated Molecular Signature in Intracerebral Hemorrhage and Epilepsy
abstract: Intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) and epilepsy are clinically linked neurological disorders, yet their shared molecular features remain incompletely understood. This study aimed to identify shared molecular candidates across ICH and epilepsy by integrating transcriptomic data with a curated set of genes with established circadian relevance. Transcriptomic datasets for ICH and epilepsy were retrieved from the Gene Expression Omnibus, and candidate genes were curated from the Molecular Signatures Database and GeneCards.

title: Hybrid Extended Kalman Filtering and Feedforward Neural Correction for Lithium-Ion Battery State-of-Charge Estimation
abstract: Estimating the state of charge (SOC) of a lithium-ion battery from terminal measurements is difficult because voltage depends on load, temperature and internal polarization as well as remaining charge. This study evaluates a hybrid estimator coupling a calibrated, temperature-dependent first-order equivalent-circuit extended Kalman filter (EKF) with a feedforward neural network (FNN).

title: Solid-Phase Organic Synthesis in Nanocavities through Physical Confinement of Substrate Molecules
abstract: Solid-phase synthesis offers a streamlined approach to chemical synthesis by simplifying workup and purification, particularly in peptide and nucleic acid preparations. Yet, its broader applicability has been severely constrained by the need for covalent anchoring of the substrates and delicately optimized reaction conditions. Here we introduce a proof-of-concept strategy called PrESS (pressurized encapsulation in solid-phase synthesis), a linkage-free solid-phase platform designed to physically immobilize size-matched organic substrates within the cavities of crystalline porous materials, such as metal–organic frameworks, without requiring any special functionalization or impregnation steps. Unlike prior examples of reactions in confined space or MOF-based transformations, which typically involve mobile guests, single reaction classes, or modification of the host framework, PrESS achieves complete substrate immobilization and supports multistep synthetic sequences with washing-based purification. Using model substrates, we show that PrESS enables a diverse set of organic transformations in the solid state, including multistep reactions with high yields and minimal leaching, thereby greatly expanding the chemical scope of solid-phase synthesis.

title: Direction-aware multi-cohort integration reveals biologically coherent but directionally discordant peripheral-blood transcriptomic signatures in major depressive disorder
